forecasts.label: Capital expenditure

in_year.label: Interest payable, as reported each quarter

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough forecasts £7.9m overspend on £258m budget, £7.7m of it in children's services
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council expects to spend £7.9m more than planned in 2026/27 on its day-to-day running costs (revenue spending: staff, services and contracts). That is 3.1% over a net budget of £258m, according to a first-quarter report to its cabinet on 1 October. Children and Young People accounts for £7.7m of the total.

The largest single line is placements for children in care, forecast to overspend by £5.2m. The budget assumed 429 children in care and 41 residential placements. The number of children in care was 444 in June, and residential placements stood at 47 in August. The average price of the last ten residential placements is £9,000 a week against £6,500 budgeted, and nine children are in placements costing more than £10,000 a week. Residential care makes up £3.2m of the £5.2m placement overspend.

If the overspend continues to the year end, the council will have to draw on its general fund reserves, the money set aside as a cushion for the unexpected. The report forecasts the balance falling from £10.5m at the start of the year to £6.7m by 31 March 2027, a 36% reduction. Total usable reserves, money the council can actually spend, are £23.7m, excluding the deficit on schools funding. Of that, £6.8m, or 29%, is ringfenced for specific purposes.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough schools grant forecast to overspend by £16.6m in 2026/27, taking deficit to £17.7m
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council expects to overspend its dedicated schools grant (the government grant that funds schools) by £16.6m in 2026/27, according to the first-quarter budget monitoring report (the in-year check of spending against budget) presented to Cabinet on 1 October. That would leave a cumulative deficit of £17.7m by 31 March 2027.

The report attributes the overspend to increased demand for Education, Health and Care Plans, the legal documents that set out support for children with special educational needs and disabilities. This spending falls under high needs, the part of school funding for those children.

The Department for Education (DfE) has committed to fund 90% of deficits held at 31 March 2026. For deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, the paper quotes the government as saying: "local authorities can expect that we will continue to take an appropriate and proportionate approach, though it will not be unlimited." From 2028/29, the report says, spending on special educational needs and disabilities is to be covered within the government's departmental expenditure limit, its fixed spending budget for departments. The papers do not say how much of the new deficit the government will fund.

news_drafts.headline: Peterborough sets up Property Board after January statutory report on John Mansfield Centre sale
news_drafts.lead:
Peterborough City Council has created an internal Property Board to scrutinise property decisions before they are taken, after its chief finance officer issued a statutory report in January 2026 on the disposal of the John Mansfield Centre. The council's Annual Governance Statement action plan, before the Audit Committee on 23 September, says oversight of decision notices on property transactions "required improvement".

The report was issued under sections 5 and 114 of the relevant legislation. A section 114 notice is a formal warning from the chief finance officer that the council cannot balance its budget, which freezes new spending until councillors agree a plan. Cabinet has since retrospectively approved four historic decisions on commercial leases that exceeded the £250,000 aggregate rental threshold.

The plan also covers procurement. An external review of the procurement function made 49 recommendations, and the council is tracking which are underway, which it regards as unattainable and which still need progressing. Temporary accommodation procurement has concluded, with 11 suppliers awarded contracts, and the council describes it as now compliant. Cabinet agreed longer-term arrangements on 23 March 2026. The council's own paper says procurement and contract management "remain areas of elevated risk".

findings.headline: Stanground Bypass Adoption Improvements: council to fund £3.189m scheme through prudential borrowing, preserving reserves, at c£400k annual cost over 12-year life
findings.detail: Stanground Bypass Adoption Improvements (£3.189m) would normally be funded from Persimmon Homes developer contribution held in earmarked reserves. Council instead proposes adding scheme to capital programme and funding through prudential borrowing. This releases £3.189m reserve funding to General Fund, reducing need for reserve drawdown against overspend. Borrowing cost c£400k per year over 12-year asset life. Cabinet recommendation explicitly justifies decision as strengthening reserves and financial resilience 'at a time of sustained financial pressure'.
findings.matters: Reverses normal councils' preference to minimise debt and use reserves. Signals that maintaining liquid reserves is now more critical priority than minimising borrowing. Decision acknowledges financial stress and need to preserve cash flexibility. Borrowing cost (£400k per year) is real but accepted as price for reserve protection.
findings.figures: £3.189m new prudential borrowing; c£400k annual financing cost; 12-year asset life; preserves £3.189m within General Fund reserves
findings.quote: It is recommended that the Stanground Bypass Adoption Improvements Scheme be added to the Council's capital programme and funded through prudential borrowing. This approach would enable the Council to retain £3.189m of the developer contribution received from Persimmon Homes, within the Councils overall reserves balances, to support the wider financial position.

findings.headline: General Fund usable reserves could reduce to £6.7m by 31 March 2027 after £7.9m overspend; total usable and ringfenced reserves £23.7m with £6.8m ringfenced for specific purposes
findings.detail: General Fund opening balance £10.5m; after £7.9m in-year overspend and including £3.2m contribution linked to Exceptional Financial Support request, forecasts show reserve could fall to £6.7m (36% reduction). Total earmarked and usable reserves £23.7m excluding DSG deficit, but £6.8m ringfenced for specific purposes (29% of total), limiting flexible use. Reserves strengthened through Flexible Use of Capital Receipts Policy (approved February 2026) but position remains vulnerable.
findings.matters: Reserve buffer has halved in proportion to budget in single year. Ringfenced reserves cannot be deployed to address shortfalls. Limited headroom creates risk that further demand shocks or forecast deterioration in Q2-Q4 would exhaust liquid reserves and require external support.
findings.figures: General Fund £10.5m opening to £6.7m projected (36% reduction); total usable reserves £23.7m (excluding DSG); ringfenced reserves £6.8m (29% of usable total)
findings.quote: However, after allowing for the £7.9m in-year overspend, current forecasts indicate that the reserve could reduce to £6.7m.

findings.headline: 37% of savings programme at red or amber risk; Culture & Leisure £0.8m savings delayed, with £0.2m now red-rated; Children's Residential Homes £0.3m programme not yet started
findings.detail: Savings programme RAG status: 27% realised (blue), 36% low risk (green), 30% moderate risk (amber), 7% high risk (red). Highest-risk programmes include Culture & Leisure £0.8m (decisions on future operating model delayed into August, value-for-money assessment ongoing, now £0.2m red and £0.6m amber); Children's Residential Homes £0.3m (programme not started, unlikely to achieve in-year due to lead-in requirements); P-Ltd Service Efficiencies £0.15m (draft transformation plan under development, savings dependent on investment and capacity decisions). All red-rated savings already incorporated as cost pressures in forecast position.
findings.matters: Over one third of savings not tracking to plan. High-profile programmes dependent on decisions still pending. If additional savings slip from green or amber to red, overspend will worsen materially beyond current £7.9m forecast.
findings.figures: 37% of savings at red/amber; Culture & Leisure £0.8m (£0.2m red, £0.6m amber); Children's Residential Homes £0.3m (red, not started); P-Ltd £0.15m (amber)
findings.quote: At the end of June, 37% of the savings are rated as red or amber and those with the greatest risk are summarised below: Culture and Leisure Savings - £0.8m - The remaining savings relating to Culture and Heritage Services remain dependent on decisions regarding the future operating model.

findings.headline: Dedicated Schools Grant deficit projected at £17.7m by 31 March 2027; government to fund 90% of historical deficit but defines future funding only as 'proportionate approach'
findings.detail: DSG overspend of £16.6m forecast due to increased Education Health and Care Plans, requiring additional special and independent school placements and SEN funding in mainstream schools. Government has committed to funding 90% of DSG deficits held at 31 March 2026. For deficits arising in 2026/27 and 2027/28, government states it will take an 'appropriate and proportionate approach, though it will not be unlimited'. From 2028/29 SEND spending to be covered within government DEL budget, removing this risk for future years.
findings.matters: Large deficit mitigated significantly by government funding (90% of historical), but future commitments for 2026/27-2027/28 remain undefined as 'proportionate'. Depending on demand levels, council could face uncompensated DSG costs in 2027/28. Long-term (2028/29+) risk eliminated by DEL inclusion.
findings.figures: £16.6m DSG overspend forecast; £17.7m DSG deficit by 31 March 2027; government funding 90% of March 2026 historic deficit; remaining 10% and future accruals under statutory override until 31 March 2028
findings.quote: For deficits that arise in 2026/27 and 2027/28, local authorities can expect that we will continue to take an appropriate and proportionate approach, though it will not be unlimited. From 2028/29, SEND spending will be covered within the government's DEL budget so local authorities will not be expected to fund future SEND costs from general funds.

findings.headline: Clare Lodge secure unit occupancy at 5 following OFSTED restrictions; recovery to 10 by December 2026 dependent on regulatory approval and staffing recruitment
findings.detail: Clare Lodge budgeted occupancy of 9.81 fell to 4 April-June due to OFSTED admission restrictions, creating £2.7m income shortfall. Restrictions now lifted; occupancy currently 5 with planned monthly increases reaching 10 by December, then 11 in January-February, 10 in March. Recovery is staged to maintain OFSTED compliance while recruiting permanent staff to replace agency cover. Young people being admitted have increasingly complex needs.
findings.matters: Significant income-dependent service currently loss-making. Recovery pathway exists but depends on regulatory approval and labour market (staff recruitment), not council control. If occupancy recovery fails to materialise, the £2.7m shortfall continues indefinitely.
findings.figures: £2.7m reduced income; occupancy 4 (April-June) vs 9.81 budgeted; current occupancy 5; target 10 by December
findings.quote: Due to OFSTED admission restrictions, occupancy at the start of the financial year was 4 and remained at 4 for May and June. Restrictions have now been lifted and occupancy is slowly rising and is currently 5.

daily_post.headline: Clare Lodge occupancy at 5 against budget of 9.81; recovery plan targets 10 by December 2026 with £2.7m income pressure
daily_post.lead: Service is dependent on regulatory compliance and staff recruitment; income forecasts rest on specific occupancy recovery plan that is not yet proven.
